ev.eth_h_yemrehanna.title: A church in a cave
ev.eth_h_yemrehanna.text: King Yemrehanna Krestos ordered a church built right inside a huge cave, in stripes of wood and stone. Craftsmen were gathered from all over Lasta, and the wonder was talked of in every market.
ev.eth_h_yemrehanna.note: The church of Yemrehanna Krestos, in a cave near Lalibela, is attributed to the Zagwe king of that name. His dates are unknown; it is usually placed in the 12th century.
ev.eth_h_lalibela_carving.title: Churches in the rock
ev.eth_h_lalibela_carving.text: King Lalibela has conceived something unheard of: to carve whole churches out of the red rock, from the top down. Villages are summoned to send workers to cut stone, carry rubble and feed the masons. Those who cannot work give grain.
ev.eth_h_lalibela_carving.note: Tradition links the eleven rock-hewn churches of Lalibela to King Lalibela (ruled c. 1181/1185–1221). The work probably took longer than one reign.
ev.eth_h_jerusalem_lost.title: Jerusalem has fallen
ev.eth_h_jerusalem_lost.text: Pilgrims have brought terrible news: Jerusalem has been taken by Sultan Salah ad-Din. The priests say King Lalibela means to build a new Jerusalem here, since the old one is now out of reach.
ev.eth_h_jerusalem_lost.note: Salah ad-Din took Jerusalem in 1187. Later tradition connects this with Lalibela's plan for a "New Jerusalem", complete with a river Jordan and a Golgotha. Historians consider the link plausible but unproven.
ev.eth_h_yekuno_amlak.title: A new king from Amhara
ev.eth_h_yekuno_amlak.text: Prince Yekuno Amlak of Amhara has overthrown the last Zagwe king. He says he descends from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, and that the throne has at last returned to the rightful line. In Lasta they grumble; in Shewa they rejoice.
ev.eth_h_yekuno_amlak.note: In 1270 Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe dynasty and founded the Solomonic dynasty, which ruled (with interruptions) until 1974. He based his claim on descent from Solomon and Makeda, the Queen of Sheba.
ev.eth_h_debre_libanos.title: Saint Takla Haymanot
ev.eth_h_debre_libanos.text: All Shewa talks of the monk Takla Haymanot: they say he prayed standing for so many years that one of his legs withered. A monastery has grown up around him in the mountains, and disciples come from all over the land.
ev.eth_h_debre_libanos.note: Takla Haymanot (c. 1215–1313) founded the monastery of Debre Asbo in Shewa, later called Debre Libanos, one of the country's chief monasteries. The tale of his years of standing prayer is part of his hagiography.
ev.eth_h_kebra_nagast.title: "The Glory of Kings"
ev.eth_h_kebra_nagast.text: The priests of Aksum are reading a new book, the Kebra Nagast, "The Glory of Kings". It tells how the Queen of Sheba bore Solomon a son, Menelik, and how he brought the Ark of the Covenant to Aksum. So God now dwells here.
ev.eth_h_kebra_nagast.note: The Kebra Nagast was compiled or translated into Ge'ez in the early 14th century; its colophon names a priest of Aksum called Yeshaq. It justified the rule of the Solomonic dynasty and the tradition of the Ark at Aksum.
ev.eth_h_amda_seyon.title: The wars of Amda Seyon
ev.eth_h_amda_seyon.text: King Amda Seyon is leading his army against the Muslim sultanates of Ifat and Adal. They say he throws himself into the thick of every fight. Men and supplies are being taken from the villages.
ev.eth_h_amda_seyon.march.success: You came back with plunder and stories of a king who knows no fear.
ev.eth_h_amda_seyon.march.failure: You were badly wounded in the very first clash.
ev.eth_h_amda_seyon.note: In 1332 Amda Seyon (1314–1344) defeated a coalition of Muslim rulers led by Sabr ad-Din of Ifat and subdued the eastern sultanates for a long time. His campaigns are described in one of the earliest Ethiopian royal chronicles.
ev.eth_h_abuna_salama.title: New books
ev.eth_h_abuna_salama.text: Abuna Salama, sent from Egypt, is having books translated from Arabic into Ge'ez: lives of the saints, commentaries, prayers. In the monasteries the copyists work from dawn to dusk.
ev.eth_h_abuna_salama.note: Metropolitan Salama II (in Ethiopia c. 1348–1388), called "the Translator", oversaw the translation of many church books from Arabic into Ge'ez, a golden age of Ethiopian letters.
ev.eth_h_zara_yaqob_crowned.title: Coronation at Aksum
ev.eth_h_zara_yaqob_crowned.text: King Zara Yaqob has come to Aksum to be crowned in the ancient way. The streets were strewn with greenery, girls sang, and the king, they say, sat on the ancient stone throne like the kings before him.
ev.eth_h_zara_yaqob_crowned.note: Zara Yaqob (1434–1468) was crowned at Aksum in 1436, reviving an ancient custom. He spent about three years in the city.
ev.eth_h_zara_yaqob_laws.title: The decrees of Zara Yaqob
ev.eth_h_zara_yaqob_laws.text: King Zara Yaqob demands that every Christian keep the feasts of the Virgin and have a confessor, and diviners and worshippers of the old spirits are punished without mercy. The king's men are inspecting the villages.
ev.eth_h_zara_yaqob_laws.grumble.success: The king's men passed you by.
ev.eth_h_zara_yaqob_laws.grumble.failure: Someone informed. You had to pay a fine.
ev.eth_h_zara_yaqob_laws.note: Zara Yaqob (1434–1468) introduced many feasts of the Virgin, required every Christian to have a confessor and harshly persecuted pagan cults and dissenters. The king himself wrote several theological works.
ev.eth_h_gomit.title: Victory at Gomit
ev.eth_h_gomit.text: Ahmad Badlay, sultan of Adal, invaded the king's lands, but at Gomit Zara Yaqob routed his army and the sultan himself was killed. Captives and plunder are led through the villages, and everyone has turned out to watch.
ev.eth_h_gomit.note: In 1445, at the battle of Gomit (Egubba), Zara Yaqob defeated the Adal sultan Shihab ad-Din Ahmad Badlay, who fell in the fighting.
ev.eth_h_debre_mitmaq.title: Peace over the Sabbaths
ev.eth_h_debre_mitmaq.text: The council of Debre Mitmaq under King Zara Yaqob has decreed that both Saturday and Sunday are to be kept holy. The disciples of Ewostatewos, persecuted for so many years, are returning to the churches, and the quarrellers have finally fallen silent.
ev.eth_h_debre_mitmaq.note: At the Council of Debre Mitmaq (1450) Zara Yaqob reconciled the church with the followers of Ewostatewos by accepting the observance of both Sabbaths.
ev.eth_h_debre_berhan.title: Mountain of light
ev.eth_h_debre_berhan.text: For several nights a wondrous light burned in the sky over Shewa. King Zara Yaqob took it as a sign, ordered a church built on the spot and set up his court beside it. The place was named Debre Berhan, "Mountain of Light".
ev.eth_h_debre_berhan.note: According to the chronicle, Zara Yaqob founded Debre Berhan after a miraculous light in the sky, usually identified with Halley's comet of 1456. The town became the king's residence in his last years.
ev.eth_h_yeshaq_decree.title: War in the mountains
ev.eth_h_yeshaq_decree.text: King Yeshaq's armies are marching on the mountains of Semien and Wogera, where the Beta Israel communities live. Refugees bring news of burned villages and seized land.
ev.eth_h_yeshaq_decree.note: King Yeshaq (1414–1429) fought the Beta Israel; chronicles credit him with stripping the unbaptised of land rights. The details are known mostly from later Christian sources.
ev.eth_h_covilha.title: A Frank at court
ev.eth_h_covilha.text: A Frank has turned up at the royal camp — a Portuguese who came to find the Christian king beyond the seas. He is treated with honour and given land and a wife, but not allowed to go home: he has seen too much.
ev.eth_h_covilha.note: The Portuguese Pêro da Covilhã reached Ethiopia around 1494, under King Eskender. He was showered with favours but never allowed to leave; the embassy of 1520 found him still there.
ev.eth_h_eleni.title: Queen Eleni
ev.eth_h_eleni.text: King Lebna Dengel is still a boy, and the old Queen Eleni rules the land. She has sent an envoy to the distant king of the Franks: together, she says, they could defeat the Muslims on sea and land.
ev.eth_h_eleni.note: Queen Eleni (d. 1522) was regent for the young Lebna Dengel (from 1508) and around 1509 sent an envoy, Matthew the Armenian, to Portugal proposing an alliance against the Muslim powers.
ev.eth_h_mahfuz.title: The death of Mahfuz
ev.eth_h_mahfuz.text: Garad Mahfuz, who raided the highlands for years, has been killed in battle with King Lebna Dengel's army. Some celebrate; others swear revenge.
ev.eth_h_mahfuz.note: In 1517 Lebna Dengel's army defeated and killed Mahfuz, governor of Zeila and war leader of Adal, who had led raids into Christian lands for years.
ev.eth_h_harar_capital.title: Harar the capital
ev.eth_h_harar_capital.text: Sultan Abu Bakr has moved his court to Harar. The city is full of soldiers, merchants and petitioners; market prices are rising and new houses are going up by the gates.
ev.eth_h_harar_capital.note: Around 1520 Sultan Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad moved the capital of Adal from Dakkar to Harar.
ev.eth_h_alvares.title: The Frankish embassy
ev.eth_h_alvares.text: A Portuguese embassy is passing through: bearded men in black with crosses and strange instruments. Their priest, Francisco Álvares, asks about everything and writes in a book.
ev.eth_h_alvares.note: A Portuguese embassy arrived in Ethiopia in 1520 and stayed six years. Its chaplain, Francisco Álvares, described the country, the court of Lebna Dengel and the churches of Lalibela in a book published in 1540.
ev.eth_h_jihad_call.title: The imam's call
ev.eth_h_jihad_call.text: Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim — whom the highlanders will call Grañ, "the Left-handed" — summons the Muslims to holy war against the Christian king. Somali and Afar warriors are streaming into Harar.
ev.eth_h_jihad_call.join.success: You came back with plunder and tales of victory.
ev.eth_h_jihad_call.join.failure: You were wounded on the first campaign.
ev.eth_h_jihad_call.note: Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi (c. 1506–1543), nicknamed Grañ ("the Left-handed"), united Adal with Somali and Afar clans and in 1529 launched a war on the Christian kingdom.
ev.eth_h_shimbra_kure.title: Shimbra Kure
ev.eth_h_shimbra_kure.text: At Shimbra Kure the great royal army has been routed by Imam Ahmad. Fugitives speak of heaps of dead, and say the roads into Shewa now lie open.
ev.eth_h_shimbra_kure.flee: Take your people into the mountains
ev.eth_h_shimbra_kure.stand.success: The enemy passed by, and you gathered the surviving neighbours.
ev.eth_h_shimbra_kure.note: In March 1529 Lebna Dengel's army suffered a crushing defeat by Imam Ahmad at Shimbra Kure, opening the way to the conquest of the highlands.
ev.eth_h_gran_shewa.title: The churches burn
ev.eth_h_gran_shewa.text: The imam's troops are burning the monasteries of Shewa — even Debre Libanos is aflame. The people are offered a choice: accept Islam or lose everything. Many agree, just to survive.
ev.eth_h_gran_shewa.resist.success: Your band fought its way out and escaped into the mountains.
ev.eth_h_gran_shewa.resist.failure: The village was taken. You survived by a miracle.
ev.eth_h_gran_shewa.note: In 1531–1535 Imam Ahmad's forces took Shewa and most of the highlands, destroying many churches and monasteries (Debre Libanos was burned in 1531). Many Christians were forcibly converted; after 1543 most returned to the church.
ev.eth_h_gran_lasta.title: The imam in Lasta
ev.eth_h_gran_lasta.text: The imam's troops have reached Lasta. The monks are hiding books and tabots in caves, and the people are retreating to the crags. They say the imam himself went to look at the rock churches.
ev.eth_h_gran_lasta.hide: Help the monks hide the relics
ev.eth_h_gran_lasta.hide.success: The tabots and books are hidden where nobody will find them.
ev.eth_h_gran_lasta.hide.failure: You were spotted. You were wounded and your house was looted.
ev.eth_h_gran_lasta.note: In 1533 Imam Ahmad's forces entered Lasta. According to the Futuh al-Habasha, the chronicle of the conquest, the imam viewed the rock churches of Lalibela; sources differ on how much they suffered.
ev.eth_h_gran_aksum.title: Mary of Zion burns
ev.eth_h_gran_aksum.text: The imam's troops have entered Aksum and burned the ancient church of Mary of Zion. People whisper that the Ark was carried away and hidden in time, and nobody but its guardian knows where.
ev.eth_h_gran_aksum.ark: Believe the Ark is safe, and pray
ev.eth_h_gran_aksum.note: Around 1535 Imam Ahmad's forces destroyed the cathedral of Mary of Zion at Aksum. Tradition holds that the Ark (tabot) was hidden in time; the cathedral was rebuilt under Fasilides in the 17th century.
ev.eth_h_harar_spoils.title: Spoils from the highlands
ev.eth_h_harar_spoils.text: Caravans of plunder are coming down from the highlands into Harar: church vessels, cloth, cattle and captives. The market is full, prices have fallen, and in the squares the imam's letters about new victories are read aloud.
ev.eth_h_harar_spoils.note: During Imam Ahmad's conquests (1529–1543) enormous spoils poured into Harar. The chronicle Futuh al-Habasha describes them in detail.
ev.eth_h_gama_arrives.title: Four hundred Franks
ev.eth_h_gama_arrives.text: Four hundred Portuguese have landed at Massawa with fire weapons — thunder that kills from afar. They are led by young Cristóvão da Gama. The queen mother Sabla Wangel came down from the mountains to meet them.
ev.eth_h_gama_arrives.note: In 1541 some 400 Portuguese musketeers led by Cristóvão da Gama, son of Vasco da Gama, landed at Massawa. The dowager queen Sabla Wangel joined them in Tigray.
ev.eth_h_gama_death.title: The death of da Gama
ev.eth_h_gama_death.text: Bitter news has come: the imam has defeated the Portuguese, and their wounded leader da Gama was captured and put to death. The surviving Franks have gone into the mountains to join the young king Galawdewos.
ev.eth_h_gama_death.note: In August 1542, after the defeat at Wofla, Cristóvão da Gama was captured and executed on Imam Ahmad's orders. The surviving Portuguese joined the army of King Galawdewos.
ev.eth_h_wayna_daga.title: Wayna Daga
ev.eth_h_wayna_daga.text: King Galawdewos and the Portuguese have defeated the imam at Wayna Daga, near Lake Tana. The imam himself was killed by a musket ball. Church gongs ring in every village, and those converted by force go to church to repent and return.
ev.eth_h_wayna_daga.note: In February 1543, at the battle of Wayna Daga, the army of Galawdewos and the Portuguese defeated the Adal army; Imam Ahmad was killed. This ended the conquest, and most converts returned to Christianity.
ev.eth_h_imam_mourned.title: The imam is dead
ev.eth_h_imam_mourned.text: The news has reached Harar: Imam Ahmad has been killed by Lake Tana and his army scattered. His widow, Bati Del Wambara, has returned to the city and, they say, vowed to marry only the man who avenges him.
ev.eth_h_imam_mourned.note: After Imam Ahmad's death in 1543 his widow Bati Del Wambara returned to Harar. Tradition says she promised her hand to whoever avenged her husband; she later married Emir Nur ibn Mujahid.
ev.eth_h_harar_wall.title: A wall around Harar
ev.eth_h_harar_wall.text: Emir Nur has ordered a high wall with gates built around Harar so that the city will never again burn in the royal army's raids. Every household must send workers or pay.
ev.eth_h_harar_wall.note: Emir Nur ibn Mujahid (ruled 1551–1567) built the wall of Harar — the Jugol — with five gates, after a devastating raid by King Galawdewos.
ev.eth_h_galawdewos_falls.title: Galawdewos falls
ev.eth_h_galawdewos_falls.text: King Galawdewos, victor over the imam, has been killed in battle with Emir Nur. They say his head was carried off to Harar. The highlands weep, while Harar celebrates its revenge.
ev.eth_h_galawdewos_falls.text.harar: Emir Nur has defeated King Galawdewos's army, and the king himself fell in battle. Harar celebrates: Imam Ahmad is avenged, and Bati Del Wambara has kept her word — she has become the emir's wife.
ev.eth_h_galawdewos_falls.note: In March 1559 King Galawdewos was killed in battle with the forces of Emir Nur ibn Mujahid in Fatagar.
ev.eth_h_oromo.title: The Oromo are coming
ev.eth_h_oromo.text: From the south, into lands emptied by the wars, come the Oromo — with herds, cavalry and their own gada system of generations. Every eight years a new age-set of warriors seeks new pastures. One valley after another is emptying.
ev.eth_h_oromo.amba: Take your people up a mountain
ev.eth_h_oromo.trade.success: Cattle for salt — the Oromo proved honest traders.
ev.eth_h_oromo.trade.failure: The bargain fell through and the goods were lost.
ev.eth_h_oromo.note: From the mid-16th century the pastoral Oromo, organised by the gada system, moved north and west and occupied large areas of Shewa, Wollo and other regions weakened by the war with Adal.
ev.eth_h_harar_oromo.title: Harar besieged
ev.eth_h_harar_oromo.text: Since Emir Nur's death the Oromo have pressed right up to Harar's gates. The gardens outside the wall are trampled, caravans are afraid to travel, and bread grows dearer every month. Nur's wall now saves the city from new enemies.
ev.eth_h_harar_oromo.note: After Nur's death (1567) Harar suffered from Oromo raids. In 1577 Imam Muhammad Jasa moved the capital of Adal to the oasis of Aussa.
ev.eth_h_massawa_ottoman.title: Turks by the sea
ev.eth_h_massawa_ottoman.text: The Ottoman Turks have seized Massawa and pushed inland towards Debarwa. The road to the sea is blocked, merchants charge three times the price, and tolls are now paid to the pasha.
ev.eth_h_massawa_ottoman.note: In 1557 the Ottomans under Özdemir Pasha took Massawa and created the province of Habesh, cutting Ethiopia off from direct access to the sea.
ev.eth_h_sarsa_dengel.title: Sarsa Dengel in the north
ev.eth_h_sarsa_dengel.text: King Sarsa Dengel has come north and defeated the Turks together with the rebel bahr negash. They say the king is young but tireless in war — against the Turks, the Oromo and defiant princes.
ev.eth_h_sarsa_dengel.note: In 1578 Sarsa Dengel (1563–1597) defeated the Ottomans and the rebellious bahr negash Yeshaq at Addi Qarro, halting the Turkish advance into the highlands.
ev.eth_h_susenyos_catholic.title: The Roman faith by decree
ev.eth_h_susenyos_catholic.text: King Susenyos has openly embraced the Roman faith, and the Latin patriarch Mendes demands that everyone be rebaptised, priests be ordained again, services be held in the Latin way and the Sabbath be forgotten. Those who refuse lose their land.
ev.eth_h_susenyos_catholic.refuse.succes: They left you alone — for now.
ev.eth_h_susenyos_catholic.refuse.failur: For your stubbornness part of your land was taken.
ev.eth_h_susenyos_catholic.outward: Nod along, and pray the old way
ev.eth_h_susenyos_catholic.note: Susenyos declared his conversion to Catholicism in 1622. Patriarch Afonso Mendes, who arrived in 1625, demanded rebaptism, reordination and the abandonment of local customs, provoking rebellions across the country.
ev.eth_h_lasta_revolt.title: Lasta rises
ev.eth_h_lasta_revolt.text: The peasants of Lasta have risen against the Roman faith and set up a king of their own. The royal army is marching on them. The priests bless the rebels in defence of the faith of their fathers.
ev.eth_h_lasta_revolt.join.success: You survived a terrible battle and made it home.
ev.eth_h_lasta_revolt.join.failure: The rebels were crushed and you were badly wounded.
ev.eth_h_lasta_revolt.note: In 1632 Susenyos's army crushed the rebel peasants of Lasta; thousands died. Shaken by the bloodshed, the king soon allowed a return to the old faith and handed power to his son Fasilides.
ev.eth_h_fasilides.title: The old faith returns
ev.eth_h_fasilides.text: "Hear ye, hear ye! The faith of our fathers has returned!" cry the heralds. The new king Fasilides has expelled the Jesuits, and the churches are holding the old services again. People sing and dance in the streets.
ev.eth_h_fasilides.note: In 1632 Susenyos abdicated, and Fasilides (1632–1667) restored the Ethiopian Church; in 1633 the Jesuits were expelled from the country.
ev.eth_h_gondar.title: Gondar
ev.eth_h_gondar.text: King Fasilides no longer roams: north of Lake Tana he is building a permanent capital, Gondar, with a castle of several storeys in stone. Masons, carpenters and porters are summoned from all over the country.
ev.eth_h_gondar.note: Around 1636 Fasilides founded Gondar, the first permanent capital in centuries. His castle, Fasil Ghebbi, was built with the help of craftsmen from India and possibly pupils of the Portuguese.
ev.eth_h_harar_emirate.title: A new emir
ev.eth_h_harar_emirate.text: Ali ibn Daud has proclaimed himself emir of Harar and rules the city on his own, answering to no one. The merchants hope the new power will bring order to the caravan roads.
ev.eth_h_harar_emirate.note: In 1647 Ali ibn Daud founded the Emirate of Harar, a dynasty that ruled the city until the Egyptian conquest of 1875.
